<reason>Both sides executed cleanly with direct A1/A2 answers and real progression. B's strongest line — that a fare split is a misleading "receipt" because costs can't be allocated per ride — was effectively dissolved by A's Rebuttal 2 pivot to the three exact cash facts (rider paid, driver got, platform retained), reducing B's case to speculative framing effects. B's best damage was the earnings-history counter to A's airport example and the utility-commission answer to Q1, but neither neutralized A's core information-asymmetry case or the sharp Q2 pressure ("why does seeing $25 kill a fair $14 trip?"). A's reversals — "if daylight invites exit, exit is deserved" and "the embarrassment is the enforcement" — framed the stakes more decisively, and A's closing crystallized the choice better. Narrow but real edge to PRO on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.1's answer to B3.1: dissolving the "misleading vs. invented number" dilemma by distinguishing cash movement from cost accounting, which stripped CON's central opening argument of its force and forced B into purely psychological ("no disclaimer survives") territory for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
